title: Is a Balance Transfer Worth the Fee? The Break-Even Math
meta_description: Is a balance transfer worth the fee? Use this break-even method with worked examples to compare total costs and avoid common 0% APR traps.
quick_answer: A balance transfer is worth the fee when staying put would cost more in interest than the fee plus any interest after the 0% period ends. Quick check: your break-even is the fee divided by one month of interest on your current card. If you'd otherwise carry the debt well past break-even and can clear it before the promo ends without new spending, the transfer likely saves money.
key_takeaways: Break-even check: divide the fee by one month of interest on your current card (balance × APR ÷ 12). Example: $150 ÷ $100 = 1.5 months.
Target payment: (balance + fee) ÷ promo months. For a safety buffer, divide by one month fewer. Don't go by the minimum payment on your statement.
If you can't finish in time, add the interest you'll pay after the promo to the fee before you compare. On a true 0% card, the transfer can still come out ahead.
Use autopay and keep new purchases off the transfer card. A late payment can bring a fee and, on some cards, end the promo early.
"No interest if paid in full" (deferred interest) is not the same as 0% APR. If you miss the deadline, interest can be charged all the way back to the start.
Skip the transfer if you could clear the debt in a month or two anyway, or if you're likely to run the old card back up.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone with a high-interest credit card balance who has a 0% balance transfer offer, or is thinking about applying for one, and wants to know in dollars whether the fee actually saves money.
intro:
A 0% balance transfer offer can look like free money until you see the fee, which is often a few percent of everything you move. Whether that fee is a good deal or a waste depends on four numbers you can find quickly: your balance, your current APR, the transfer fee and how long the promo lasts.

This guide covers a simple break-even method, a worked example with clearly labeled example numbers, a payoff tracker you can copy and the fine-print traps that can quietly wipe out your savings. It uses US-style card terms. Fees, rules and consumer protections differ by country and by issuer, so always check your own card's terms.

steps.name: Collect your numbers
steps.text: From your current statement, write down the balance, the APR and the monthly payment you can reliably afford. From the new card's pricing and terms (in the US, usually a table called the Schumer box), note: the intro APR on transfers, how many months it lasts, the fee percentage and any minimum fee, the regular APR after the promo, the deadline for making transfers, and whether the promo starts when the account opens or when the transfer posts.

steps.name: Calculate the transfer fee
steps.text: Multiply the amount you plan to move by the fee percentage. If the card charges whichever is greater of a percentage or a flat minimum, use the higher figure. Example: $5,000 × 3% = $150. The fee is usually added to your new balance, so in this example you would owe $5,150.

steps.name: Estimate what staying put would cost
steps.text: For a quick figure, work out one month of interest on your current card: balance × APR ÷ 12. Example: $5,000 × 24% ÷ 12 = about $100. For the full picture, enter your balance, APR and planned payment into a free credit card payoff calculator. Example: clearing $5,000 in 15 months at 24% APR takes about $389 a month and costs roughly $837 in interest.

steps.name: Find your break-even point
steps.text: Divide the fee by one month of interest on your current card. Example: $150 ÷ $100 = 1.5 months. Then compare that with how long you'd actually carry the debt without a transfer. Breaking even at 1.5 months on a debt you'd carry for 15 months is a clear win. Breaking even at 1.5 months on a debt you'd clear in 2 months is not.

steps.name: Work out the payment that clears the balance before 0% ends
steps.text: Divide the new balance (including the fee) by the number of promo months. Example: $5,150 ÷ 15 ≈ $344 a month. To finish one month early as a buffer, divide by 14 instead: about $368 a month. Use this figure, not the minimum payment on your statement.

steps.name: Stress-test for a shortfall
steps.text: If that payment doesn't fit your budget, multiply what you can afford by the number of promo months and subtract the result from the new balance to see what's left. Then estimate the interest on that leftover amount at the regular APR. Example: $250 × 15 = $3,750, which leaves about $1,400. At an example 25% APR, that adds roughly $104 in interest. Add it to the fee and compare the total with staying on your current card.

steps.name: Weigh the costs that aren't in dollars
steps.text: Factor in the small, temporary credit score dip from a new application. Check whether the offer uses deferred interest (look for "if paid in full" wording). Be honest about whether you'll keep using the old card. If any of these tip the balance, the dollar savings may not be worth it.

steps.name: Request the transfer correctly
steps.text: Many issuers let you request a transfer during the application, or later through a balance transfer option in the card's app or website. You'll typically need the old card's issuer, its account number and the amount to move. Request the transfer inside the transfer window, make sure the amount plus the fee fits within your new credit limit, and save the confirmation.

steps.name: Set guardrails if you go ahead
steps.text: Set autopay for your full planned payment, or at least the minimum. Add calendar reminders 90 and 30 days before the promo ends. Keep paying the old card on time until the transfer shows as posted. Remove the old card from saved payment methods and digital wallets so new spending doesn't creep back.

sections.heading: Is a balance transfer worth the fee? Use the break-even rule
paragraphs: A balance transfer is worth the fee when the interest it saves is larger than the fee plus any interest you'll pay after the promotional rate ends. The rest of this guide puts real numbers on that rule.

A balance transfer moves debt from one credit card to another. Usually the new card offers a low or 0% introductory APR on transferred balances for a set number of months. In return, most issuers charge a one-time balance transfer fee. It's typically a percentage of the amount you move and is added to your new balance when the transfer posts.

The fastest test is the break-even point: how many months of interest on your current card it takes to equal the fee. To find it, divide the fee by one month of interest on your current card (balance × APR ÷ 12). Then compare that with how long you'd realistically carry the debt without a transfer. If you'd carry it much longer than the break-even point, the fee is usually small next to the savings.

Treat break-even as a rough first check, not the final answer. As you pay the balance down, the interest falls a little each month. To actually decide, compare the total cost of each option over the same payoff period, as the steps in this guide do.
bullets: Intro (promo) APR: the temporary rate on transferred balances, often 0%, for a fixed number of months.
Balance transfer fee: a one-time charge, usually a percentage of the amount moved, sometimes with a minimum dollar amount.
Regular (go-to) APR: the rate that applies to any balance left when the promo ends.
Transfer window: the period after the account opens during which transfers qualify for the promo rate.
Break-even months: the fee ÷ one month of interest on your current card.

sections.heading: Worked example: $5,000 at 24% APR (example numbers)
paragraphs: In this example, moving a $5,000 balance to a 0% card with a 3% fee saves roughly $690 compared with clearing the same debt over 15 months on the current card. These numbers are illustrations, not real offers. Your own rates and fees will differ.

The setup: your current card has a $5,000 balance at an example APR of 24%. The new card offers an example 0% intro APR on transfers for 15 months, a 3% fee and a 25% regular APR after the promo. The estimates use monthly compounding. Most cards calculate interest daily, so real totals will differ slightly.

Staying put: clearing $5,000 in 15 months at 24% APR takes about $389 a month and costs roughly $837 in interest. A free online credit card payoff calculator will give you a similar estimate for your own numbers.

Transferring: the 3% fee is $150, so your new balance is $5,150. Spread over 15 months, that's about $344 a month, and the fee is the only cost of borrowing. That's about $687 less than staying put, with a monthly payment roughly $45 lower.

Break-even: one month of interest on the current card is about $100 ($5,000 × 24% ÷ 12), so the $150 fee equals about 1.5 months of interest. You'd otherwise carry this debt for 15 months, so the fee is easily covered, as long as you pay on time and don't add new debt.
bullets: Payment to clear in 15 months: $5,150 ÷ 15 ≈ $344
Payment to clear one month early: $5,150 ÷ 14 ≈ $368
Staying on the 24% card: about $389 a month and about $837 in interest
Estimated saving with a 3% fee: about $687
With an example 5% fee ($250), the transfer still costs about $587 less in this scenario

sections.heading: What if you can't pay it off before the 0% period ends?
paragraphs: If you can't clear the balance before the promo ends, a transfer to a true 0% APR card can still save money. Before you compare, add the interest you'll pay after the promo to the fee.

Take the same example with a smaller budget: you can only afford $250 a month. After 15 months you've paid $3,750, which leaves about $1,400. At the example 25% regular APR, that takes about six more months and roughly $104 in interest to clear, for a total cost of around $254 over about 21 months. Paying the same $250 a month on the original 24% card would take about 26 months and cost roughly $1,450 in interest.

The math turns against a transfer when the balance is small and you'd clear it quickly anyway. Example: $1,000 at 24% APR, paid off at $500 a month, costs only about $30 in interest over two months. A 3% fee ($30) or a 5% fee ($50) cancels out the saving, and the application still adds a hard inquiry to your credit report.
A transfer also looks weaker when the fee is high and the promo is short. The same applies if you expect to carry a large leftover balance at a regular APR that's higher than your current card's.
bullets: Red flag: breaking even takes up a large share of the promo period.
Red flag: you could pay the balance off in one to three months without a transfer.
Red flag: the required payment is well beyond what your budget can reliably cover, and the new card's regular APR is higher than your current one.
Red flag: the offer's terms mention deferred interest or "if paid in full" conditions.

sections.heading: The fine-print traps that can wipe out your savings
paragraphs: The biggest risks with a balance transfer usually come from the card's terms, not the fee. New purchases, late payments, timing rules and credit limits can each erase the savings you calculated.

Read the offer's pricing and terms before you apply, and the cardholder agreement once you're approved. Look specifically for how purchases are charged, what happens if you pay late and when the promo period starts.
bullets: New purchases: the 0% rate often applies only to transferred balances, so purchases may be charged the regular APR. On many cards, carrying any balance, even a 0% one, also removes the interest-free grace period on purchases, so interest starts right away. The simplest fix is to keep spending off the transfer card.

Late or missed payments: depending on the card's terms and where you live, a late payment can bring a late fee. On some cards it can also end the promo rate early or trigger a higher penalty APR. Autopay for at least the minimum is your safety net.
Paying only the minimum: the minimum payment on a 0% balance is usually far below what you need to finish in time. Pay the target you calculated instead.
The promo clock: the 0% period may start when the account opens, not when the transfer posts. Transfers often have to be requested within a set window to qualify.
Same-bank transfers: issuers usually don't allow transfers between two cards they issue.
Your credit limit: you won't know your limit until you're approved, and the fee usually counts against it, so you may only be able to move part of the balance.
The gap before posting: transfers can take several days or longer. Keep paying the old card on time until its balance shows as paid.

sections.heading: Deferred-interest store cards are not the same as 0% APR
paragraphs: Deferred-interest offers are common on store cards and retail financing, and they work differently from a 0% intro APR. If any balance remains when the deadline passes, you can be charged all the interest that built up since the original purchase date.

The wording is the clue. A true intro APR offer says something like "0% intro APR for X months." A deferred-interest offer usually says "no interest if paid in full within X months." With the first, interest is charged only on what's left after the promo ends. With the second, interest is tracked in the background the whole time and added to your balance if you miss the target, even by a small amount.

A simplified example (example numbers): you make a $1,200 purchase on 12 months of deferred interest at an example 30% APR. You pay $100 a month for 11 months, which leaves $100 at the deadline. Interest was tracked on the falling balance all year, so roughly $195 is charged back on a debt that was almost gone.

If you already have a deferred-interest balance, moving it to a true 0% balance transfer card before the deadline can make sense. First confirm that the new issuer accepts the transfer and that it will post before the deferred-interest date.
bullets: "0% intro APR": interest is charged only on the balance left after the promo.
"No interest if paid in full": interest can be charged back to the purchase date.
Aim to clear any deferred-interest balance at least one statement before the deadline.

sections.heading: How a balance transfer can affect your credit score
paragraphs: Opening a new card for a balance transfer usually causes a small, temporary dip in your credit score. Over the longer term, what matters most is paying on time and bringing the balance down.
These effects pull in different directions, so the exact impact is hard to predict and varies by person and scoring model. Your credit report or monitoring service can show which factors changed.
bullets: Hard inquiry: applying usually triggers one, which can lower your score slightly for a limited time.
Newer accounts: a brand-new account lowers the average age of your accounts.
Overall utilization: a new credit limit can lower the share of your total available credit that you're using, which tends to help.
Per-card utilization: if the transfer uses most of the new card's limit, that card looks nearly maxed out. Some scoring models count that against you until it's paid down.

Closing the old card: this removes its limit from your total, which can push overall utilization up. Some people keep it open with a zero balance (watch for annual fees); others close it to remove the temptation.
Payment history: on-time payments typically matter most, which is another reason to use autopay.

sections.heading: A simple payoff tracker to keep the transfer on schedule
paragraphs: A balance transfer only pays off if you hit a fixed monthly target. A one-page tracker shows you within a month or two whether you're falling behind.

You can build it in a spreadsheet, a notes app or a workspace tool. Set it up the day the transfer posts, and use the exact promo end date from your terms or statement, not the month you think it ends.
bullets: Starting balance: the amount transferred plus the fee (example: $5,150).
Promo end date: copied from your card terms or statement.
Target payment: starting balance ÷ (promo months − 1). Example: $5,150 ÷ 14 ≈ $368.
Target balance: starting balance − (target payment × months elapsed). Example after 6 months: $5,150 − $2,208 = $2,942.
Actual balance: taken from each statement. If it's above target, raise next month's payment or cut spending elsewhere.
Old card balance: this should stay at $0. Any new charge is an early warning sign.
Check-ins: 90 and 30 days before the promo ends, look at what's left and decide how you'll finish.

sections.heading: Who a balance transfer is not for (and what to consider instead)
paragraphs: A balance transfer is a poor fit for anyone likely to run the old card back up. They can end up with two balances and a fee instead of one balance at a lower rate.

A transfer is also a weak choice in three other cases. The first is if you could clear the debt in a month or two anyway. The second is if you can't commit to a fixed payment big enough to make real progress. The third is if you're unlikely to qualify for a strong offer: a denial still costs a hard inquiry, and an approval may come with a limit too low to help.

This guide is general information, not personal financial advice. Card terms, fees and consumer protections differ by country and issuer. Check your card agreement and your local regulator, such as the CFPB in the US or the FCA in the UK. For your own situation, talk to a licensed adviser or a nonprofit credit counselor.
bullets: Ask your current issuer for a lower APR or about a hardship program. There's no application or fee, but approval isn't guaranteed.
Personal consolidation loan: a fixed payment and end date, but there may be an origination fee, and the rate depends on your credit.
Debt management plan through a nonprofit credit counseling agency: may lower the rates on enrolled cards, but often involves a monthly fee and closing those accounts.
Avalanche method: pay the minimum on every card and put any extra toward the highest-APR card first. You open no new accounts, but you keep paying full interest along the way.

recommendations.best_for: Readers who want a single page to track a balance transfer payoff plan, with the starting balance, promo end date, monthly target vs. actual balance and check-in dates, especially if they already use Notion for other planning. Confirm current plans and features on Notion's site.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who just needs the basics. A free spreadsheet, your card issuer's payment alerts and a calendar reminder do the same job. Notion doesn't know your card's terms, so you'll typically enter balances and build any formulas yourself.

recommendations.best_for: Freelancers and small-business owners moving a business credit card balance who need the transfer fee, interest and payments recorded properly in their books. Ask your accountant how to categorize these costs, and confirm current plans and pricing on Intuit's site.
recommendations.not_for: Personal credit card debt. It's small-business accounting software, so for a household payoff plan a spreadsheet or personal budgeting app is simpler and cheaper.

faq.question: How much is a typical balance transfer fee?
faq.answer: Balance transfer fees are usually a percentage of the amount you move. On US cards, 3% to 5% is a common example range. Some cards also set a minimum dollar fee, and a few offers advertise no transfer fee, sometimes with a shorter promo period. Fees change often, so confirm the current figure in the offer's pricing and terms before you apply.

faq.question: Does a balance transfer hurt your credit score?
faq.answer: Applying for a new card usually causes a small, temporary dip because of the hard inquiry and the newer average age of your accounts. Over time, paying on time and lowering your balance tend to help more than opening the account hurts. Closing the old card can raise your utilization, so weigh that before you close it.

faq.question: What happens if I don't pay off the balance before the 0% APR ends?
faq.answer: On a true 0% intro APR card, the regular APR typically applies to whatever balance remains from that point on. You aren't charged interest for the promo months. Deferred-interest offers are different: if you don't pay in full by the deadline, they can charge interest back to the original purchase date. Your card's terms tell you which type you have.

faq.question: Do I get the balance transfer fee back if I pay off the balance early?
faq.answer: Generally no. The fee is usually charged when the transfer posts and added to your balance, so paying early doesn't get it back. That's why the break-even check matters: if you could clear the debt in a month or two, the fee may cost more than the interest you'd save.

faq.question: Should I close my old card after a balance transfer?
faq.answer: It depends on your habits and the card's costs. Keeping the old card open with a zero balance preserves its credit limit and account history, which can help your utilization, but watch for annual fees. If you know you'd be tempted to use it, removing it from digital wallets or closing it may be the safer choice.

faq.question: Is a no-fee balance transfer always the better deal?
faq.answer: Not always. If you can't finish in time, a no-fee offer with a short promo can cost more overall than an offer with a fee and a longer promo, because you'll pay the regular APR on a large leftover balance. Compare the total cost of each offer (fee plus any interest after the promo) at the monthly payment you can actually afford.

conclusion: A balance transfer is worth the fee when three things line up. First, the fee is a small fraction of the interest you'd otherwise pay. Second, you can afford a payment that clears most or all of the balance before the 0% period ends. Third, you won't add new debt on either card. Before you apply, work out four numbers: the fee, the interest on your current card, the monthly payment you'd need and any interest after the promo. If you go ahead, protect your savings with autopay, a simple tracker, reminders well before the deadline and a firm no-new-purchases rule. If the numbers or your habits don't support a transfer, asking your issuer for a lower rate, taking a consolidation loan or talking to a nonprofit credit counselor may work better. Run the same total-cost comparison on each option. This is general information; for decisions about your own situation, check your local regulator or speak with a licensed adviser.
